summary: This proposed standard defines how SNMPv2 maps onto an initial set of transport domains, meaning the underlying protocols used to carry its messages. It was replaced by RFC 1906.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP messages need a vehicle to ride on. This paper explains which vehicles can carry SNMPv2 messages.

how do you address an snmp agent
subtitle: How SNMPv2 rides on different network transport protocols.

tldr.problem: SNMPv2 messages need a way to travel between management stations and network devices. Different network environments use different underlying transport protocols.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC maps SNMPv2 onto four transport domains: UDP (preferred), OSI, AppleTalk (DDP), and IPX, plus a proxy to communicate with SNMPv1 over UDP.
tldr.outcome: SNMPv2 can interoperate across diverse networks. It was superseded by RFC 1906, which updated the mappings.

today: RFC 1449 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 1906, which updated the transport mappings for SNMPv2 and later became part of the SNMPv3 framework. The core concepts remain valid, but modern SNMP implementations use RFC 1906 and SNMPv3.

sections.title: What Transport Mappings Are
sections.content:
Network management requires a way to carry SNMPv2 messages between management stations (the controllers) and agents (the devices being managed). Different networks use different underlying protocols to carry traffic. This RFC defines how SNMPv2 messages are mapped onto four transport protocol families, allowing SNMP to work across diverse network infrastructures.

UDP is the preferred mapping because it is simple and widely available. However, some environments use OSI, AppleTalk, or IPX as their primary transport, so SNMPv2 provides mappings for those as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Management messages need a vehicle to ride on. This document tells you which vehicles (UDP, OSI, AppleTalk, IPX) can carry SNMPv2 messages.

sections.title: The Four Transport Domains
sections.content:
SNMPv2 defines a transport domain for each underlying protocol family. Each domain specifies how to address recipients and how to serialize messages.

The RFC defines four main transport domains: snmpUDPDomain for UDP (the standard), snmpCLNSDomain and snmpCONSDomain for OSI connectionless and connection-oriented modes, snmpDDPDomain for AppleTalk, and snmpIPXDomain for IPX. Each has its own addressing format and configuration parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Each transport protocol has a code name and a way of writing addresses, like how 'UDP' uses an IP address plus a port number.

sections.title: UDP: The Preferred Choice
sections.content:
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is the primary transport for SNMPv2. A UDP address is 6 octets: the first 4 octets hold an IP address in network byte order, and the last 2 hold a UDP port number.

By convention, SNMP agents listen on UDP port 161, and notification sinks (which receive asynchronous alerts from devices) listen on port 162. The minimum message size is 484 octets. UDP transport is stateless and simple, making it the natural choice for SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP is simple and fast: you give it an IP address and a port number, it sends the message as a single packet. Agents use port 161, alerts use port 162.

sections.title: Alternative Transports: OSI, AppleTalk, and IPX
sections.content:
OSI provides two modes: CLNS (connectionless) and CONS (connection-oriented). An OSI address begins with the length of an NSAP (Network Service Access Point), followed by the NSAP itself (3 to 20 octets) and a TSEL (transport service element), for a total of up to 85 octets.

AppleTalk (DDP) is unusual: because AppleTalk nodes do not have stable network addresses, SNMPv2 over DDP uses NBP names instead. An NBP address encodes an object name, type, and zone. Agents use DDP socket 8, notification sinks use socket 9.

IPX (Novell NetWare) works similarly to UDP: a 12-octet address holds a network number, physical address (MAC), and socket number. Agents listen on IPX socket 36879 (hex 900f), notification sinks on socket 36880 (hex 9010). Minimum message size for IPX is 546 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks use different plumbing: OSI uses long network names, AppleTalk uses service names instead of addresses because they change on reboot, and IPX is similar to UDP with different port numbers.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility with SNMPv1
sections.content:
To ensure interoperability, SNMPv2 defines a proxy mode for SNMPv1 communities. The transport domain rfc1157Domain allows an SNMPv2 entity to proxy SNMPv1 messages: it uses UDP with a 6-octet address (IP plus port) and employs the rfc1157noAuth authentication mechanism, which maps to an SNMPv1 community string.

This allows SNMPv2-capable management stations to manage older SNMPv1-only devices by translating between the two protocol versions. A network can thus support both SNMP generations during migration.
sections.plainLanguage: This feature lets SNMPv2 managers talk to old SNMPv1 equipment by translating their messages back and forth, like an interpreter at a business meeting.
